Applications, such as that of Watson,3 could provide accurate diagnosis through recording symptoms, based on case precedents found in databases or the internet, which will prevent expensive and time-consuming visits to doc- tors. Doctors may well become obsolete, as applications will allow users to test their blood for hundreds of diseases, or wear glasses plugged directly into their smartphones that detect life threatening diseases, such as cancer. Whatever the case, fewer will go to general medical doctors, preferring to have online consultations with specialists through video chats, which already exist for peo- ple living too far from a doctor. Organs will be printed 3D on demand within an hour and surgery will also be more automated. This will involve less invasive techniques, such a keyhole surgery and greater precision owing to robot inter- vention, which is already widely found in hospitals across the world. Moreover, AI will result in fewer human errors caused by such things as fatigue during long hours of interventions.

This might be the beginning of better and cheaper diagnosis, found person- ally, using one’s cellphone smart tech. Regarding which, LifeHand Billiscreen4 new innovative technology can detect pancreas cancer in the eyes with a cell- phone’s camera and its related application. In the near future, robot pharma- cists will sell medications targeting just the right illness and bandages will be able to administer a dose of medication based on the size and severity of an external wound. riba, iward, ernie and other robots can successfully per- form nurses and pharmacists’ work.5 The robot Xiao Yi successfully passed the doctors exam in China with a high score and is therefore, officially entitled to practice.6 Human doctors specialized in rare diseases will become much more expensive than robotic ones. As for the robot surgeons that already exist, their work is precise, but still too slow. The Vinci Surgical System and ares7 ingestible robots can assist during difficult medical procedures. The first dental surgery was performed on a human by a robot in China in 20178 and it would appear that this type of operation will become commonplace. The iRobot’s rp-vita (Remote Presence – Virtual Independent Telemedicine Assistant) can allow doctors to treat their patients without being physically present.9 This is quite a revolution. for it can treat patients with infectious disease safely diseases and in the case where a doctor is still at home or on vacation and personal input is needed in an emergency, this can now take place. During the Covid-19 world- wide pandemic, Rwanda deployed robots named Mwiza, Ikizere, Akazuba, Urumuri and Ngabo, designed to limit the exposure healthcare workers get to virus cases, and to assist infected patients in a safe manner.10

Robots can provide more autonomy to the sick, elderly, or disabled persons. They can offer mobility and a restoring sensation through bionic prostheses. Robot therapists and online therapy services may become an emerging mar- ket. Regarding which, people might feel more at ease talking to a machine that cannot judge them. This could prove extremely useful for soldiers with post- traumatic stress disorders, who are often loathed to express their feelings out loud to others. Initial successes with this technology have been demonstrated with patients with paranoid hallucinations. They were asked to design the per- secutor they faced in their mind and converse with it, in order to progressively learn to moderate such destructive behavior. Lower levels of hallucinations and vocal threats were achieved with these patients.11

We could use advanced AI to identify health issues in advance by analyzing genomes to understand epigenetics and dna change. The risk is to create a huge gap between classes as can be seen in the movie Elysium,25 when only the rich can afford technology’s advantages. This risk, called the: ‘digital divide’, pertains to where only a small percentage of the population will be able to succeed in the new technological era. Moreover, rejuvenating our cells with nanotechnologies could make us immortal, which would potentially lead to overpopulation.

Eventually, machines will be able to fix themselves and even reproduce. When this happens, we are likely to be left on our own. Hawking expressed concern that machines might “take over the world”26 someday and recom- mended to “genetically engineer humans”27 in order to keep pace with Artificial Intelligence. To maintain control of technology past the ‘Singularity’ stage, as predicted by many, human enhancement seems to be a key element. There will be several ways to ‘upgrade’ and amplify a human being, such as plastic surgery, ‘cyborgs’ prostheses, silicon injections as well as implanting sensors and computers under one’s skin.28 Would enhancing man with cyborg technol- ogies in fact trigger the arrival of a new transhumanist species? If we no longer need a heart, then the entire human body will have been redesigned and we will no longer need several organs since we will no longer have blood running through our veins to operate our body’s vital functions.

With time, we will know more about the human brain, in particular with regards to the activity of neurons and we will thus be able model one easily. As we understand better how brain works, we will be able to add neurons, raise iq s, and comprehend how some brains diseases work, such as Alzheimers, and be able to cure them. It seems realistic to predict that humans will, in a few decades, be intellectually smarter through cognitive enhancement pills, or implants that will increase their iq, or their brain-computer interface. In Cyber-Humans, Barfield Woodrow forecasts that: “Future prosthetic devices will be for the brain in terms of enhancing memory, providing access to information, allowing telepathic communication, and leading to through control of devices external to the body.”29 dna selection will allow people to define the physical characteristics of their new-born and advances in neurosciences will help him select the right neurons to deliver the desired abilities. That is, of course, only if we continue having children in the current primitive way. We may well choose our offspring to grow in incubators after sampling hair from the future parents.

Whilst James Barrat, author of Our Final Invention: Artificial Intelligence and the End of the Human Era said the following about the rise of Artificial Intelligence: “So when there is something smarter than us on the planet, it will rule over us on the planet”.32 Woodrow Barfield states correctly, in my opinion, that: “It seems to me that a human-machine merger would avoid this negative outcome.”33 According to Nick Bostrom, in Superintelligence: “Opportunities for private individuals to reduce the overall amount of existential risk from a potential intelligence explo- sion are therefore greater in the scenario in which big players remain relatively oblivious to the issue, or in which the early efforts of activists make a major differ- ence to whether, when, which, or with what attitude big players enter the game”, and “International coordination is more likely, if global governance structures are generally stronger. Coordination might also be more likely, if the significance of an intelligence explosion is widely appreciated ahead of time and if effective mon- itoring of all serious projects is feasible.”34

Whilst it will take many years to create a substantial community of super- intelligence on the planet, Woodrow Barfield suggests that before the use of telepathic communication happens at all: “umanity should engage in a debate focusing on three vital questions:
(1) whether there should be a limit placed on enhancing, augmenting, or replacing human biological parts?
(2) whether or not we should create machines that are superior in intelli- gence to unenhanced people? and
(3) whether or not we should continue to evolve on a separate path from artificially intelligent machines?”35

Nick Bostrom writes in Superintelligence: “In whole brain emulation (also known as “uploading”), intelligent software would be produced by scanning and closely modelling the computational structure of a biological brain.”36 Should we just combine and upload our minds into gigantic computers, thereby reproducing our memories, mental and intellectual characteristics and thus, preserve our species from extinction. We might even be able to upload our brain into a new body, as seen in the Netflix series Altered Carbon.37
